question: A tank endorsement is required for a Class A or B CDL driver who wants to haul a liquid or liquid gas in a tank meeting which capacity thresholds?
choice_a: An individual rated capacity of more than 55 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 500 gallons or more
choice_b: An individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1000 gallons or more
choice_c: Any capacity, regardless of size
choice_d: An aggregate rated capacity of 5000 gallons or more only
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required if the vehicle needs a Class A or B CDL and you want to haul a liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks having an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1000 gallons or more that is permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, Introduction

question: Does the liquid or gas hauled in a tank requiring a tank endorsement have to be a hazardous material?
choice_a: Only if the tank exceeds 5000 gallons
choice_b: Yes, it must always be classified as hazardous
choice_c: Only for tanks mounted on Class C vehicles
choice_d: No, the liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material
explanation: The manual specifically states: "The liquid or gas does not have to be a hazardous material."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, Introduction

question: When is a tank endorsement also required for Class C vehicles?
choice_a: When the vehicle is used to transport hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in the described rated tanks
choice_b: Only when hauling dry bulk cement
choice_c: Whenever the vehicle exceeds 10,000 pounds GVWR
choice_d: Never, tank endorsements do not apply to Class C vehicles
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is also required for Class C vehicles when the vehicle is used to transport hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in the above described rated tanks.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, Introduction

question: What should you do before loading, unloading, or driving a tanker?
choice_a: Remove the manhole covers to check the liquid level
choice_b: Inspect the vehicle to make sure it is safe to carry the liquid or gas and safe to drive
choice_c: Disconnect the grounding and bonding cables
choice_d: Fill the tank completely so there is no room for surge
explanation: The manual states that before loading, unloading, or driving a tanker, you should inspect the vehicle to make sure it is safe to carry the liquid or gas and is safe to drive.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, Introduction

question: On all tank vehicles, what does the manual say is the most important item to check?
choice_a: Tire pressure
choice_b: Leaks
choice_c: Mirror alignment
choice_d: Fuel level
explanation: The manual states: "On all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 - Leaks

question: What happens if you carry liquids or gases in a leaking tank?
choice_a: Nothing, as long as the leak is reported at the next scheduled stop
choice_b: You must pay a small fine but may continue the trip
choice_c: It is only recorded as a minor infraction
choice_d: It is a crime; you will be cited, prevented from driving further, and may be liable for clean-up of any spill
explanation: The manual states you should not carry liquids or gases in a leaking tank -- to do so is a crime. You will be cited and prevented from driving further, and you may also be liable for the clean-up of any spill.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 - Leaks

question: Besides the tank's body or shell, what else should be checked for leaks, especially around joints?
choice_a: The cab's door seals
choice_b: The fifth wheel coupling only
choice_c: The trailer suspension springs
choice_d: Pipes, connections, and hoses
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check pipes, connections, and hoses for leaks, especially around joints.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 - Leaks

question: What must you make sure of regarding the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle?
choice_a: That they are removed for cleaning
choice_b: That they are in the correct position
choice_c: That they are fully open at all times
choice_d: That they are painted a bright warning color
explanation: The manual states to check the intake, discharge, and cut-off valves and make sure the valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading, or moving the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.1 - Leaks

topic: Inspecting Tank Vehicles - Special Purpose Equipment
question: Which items does the manual list as special purpose equipment to check if your tank vehicle has them?
choice_a: GPS navigation and satellite radio
choice_b: Backup camera and blind-spot monitor
choice_c: Vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher
choice_d: Auxiliary heater and sleeper berth
explanation: The manual lists vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built in fire extinguisher as special purpose equipment to check.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 - Check Special Purpose Equipment

topic: Inspecting Tank Vehicles - Special Purpose Equipment
question: You should never drive a tank vehicle under which condition?
choice_a: With open valves or manhole covers
choice_b: With a full fuel tank
choice_c: With the radio on
choice_d: With cruise control engaged
explanation: The manual states: "Never drive a tank vehicle with open valves or manhole covers."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.2 - Check Special Purpose Equipment

topic: Inspecting Tank Vehicles - Manhole Covers and Vents
question: What should you check about manhole covers and vents on a tank vehicle?
choice_a: That the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and that the vents are kept clear so they work correctly
choice_b: That the vents are sealed shut with tape
choice_c: That the covers are painted to match the cab
choice_d: That the covers are removed before every trip
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to check manhole covers and vents: make sure the covers have gaskets and close correctly, and keep the vents clear so they work correctly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1 - Inspecting Tank Vehicles

question: Regarding required emergency equipment, what should you find out and verify before driving a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Only whether the fire extinguisher is present
choice_b: What equipment you're required to carry, and make sure you have it and that it works
choice_c: Nothing; emergency equipment is optional on tank vehicles
choice_d: Only whether the vehicle has a spare tire
explanation: The manual states to check the emergency equipment required for your vehicle -- find out what equipment you're required to carry and make sure you have it (and it works).
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.1.3 - Special Equipment

question: What does "high center of gravity" mean for a tank vehicle?
choice_a: The vehicle has an unusually light cargo load
choice_b: The vehicle's engine is mounted higher than normal
choice_c: Much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over
choice_d: The tank is mounted below the frame rails
explanation: The manual defines high center of gravity as meaning much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, which makes the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 - High Center of Gravity

question: What have tests shown about liquid tankers and posted curve speed limits?
choice_a: Tankers are safer than other vehicles at posted curve speeds
choice_b: Posted curve speeds are always set too low for tankers
choice_c: Curve speed has no effect on tanker stability
choice_d: Tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves
explanation: The manual states tests have shown that tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 - High Center of Gravity

question: How should you take highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Slightly above the posted speed for momentum
choice_b: Well below the posted speeds
choice_c: Speed is irrelevant for tank vehicles on curves
choice_d: At exactly the posted speed limit
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to take highway curves and on ramp/off ramp curves well below the posted speeds.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.1 - High Center of Gravity

question: What causes liquid surge in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Driving only on dry, level pavement
choice_b: Movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks
choice_c: A tank that is loaded completely full with no outage
choice_d: Using only baffled tanks
explanation: The manual states: "Liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 - Danger of Surge

question: What happens to the liquid in a tank when the vehicle is coming to a stop?
choice_a: It drains entirely to the rear of the tank
choice_b: It surges back and forth
choice_c: It has no effect on vehicle handling
choice_d: It immediately settles and stops moving
explanation: The manual states that for example, when coming to a stop, the liquid will surge back and forth.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 - Danger of Surge

question: When a surge wave hits the end of the tank, what does it tend to do?
choice_a: Stabilize the vehicle's handling
choice_b: Automatically apply the vehicle's brakes
choice_c: Have no effect on the truck
choice_d: Push the truck in the direction the wave is moving
explanation: The manual states that when the wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 - Danger of Surge

question: If a tank truck is stopped on a slippery surface such as ice, what can a surge wave do?
choice_a: Cause the brakes to lock automatically
choice_b: Cause the truck to accelerate forward safely
choice_c: Nothing, since the truck is already stopped
choice_d: Shove the stopped truck out into an intersection
explanation: The manual states that if the truck is on a slippery surface such as ice, the wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.2 - Danger of Surge

question: What are bulkheads used for in some liquid tanks?
choice_a: To filter contaminants out of the liquid
choice_b: To prevent the tank from leaking
choice_c: To divide the tank into several smaller tanks
choice_d: To increase overall tank capacity
explanation: The manual states some liquid tanks are divided into several smaller tanks by bulkheads.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.3 - Bulkheads

question: When loading and unloading the smaller tanks created by bulkheads, what must the driver pay attention to?
choice_a: Weight distribution, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_b: The number of passengers in the cab
choice_c: The outside air temperature only
choice_d: The color of the liquid
explanation: The manual states that when loading and unloading the smaller tanks, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and not put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.3 - Bulkheads

question: What do baffled liquid tanks have inside them?
choice_a: Bulkheads with holes that let the liquid flow through
choice_b: An automatic pressure release valve
choice_c: A built-in heating system
choice_d: A double-walled insulated shell
explanation: The manual states baffled liquid tanks have bulkheads in them with holes that let the liquid flow through.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.4 - Baffled Tanks

question: What do the baffles in a baffled tank help control?
choice_a: Engine temperature
choice_b: Fuel consumption
choice_c: Tire pressure
choice_d: The forward and backward liquid surge
explanation: The manual states the baffles help to control the forward and backward liquid surge.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.4 - Baffled Tanks

question: Even in a baffled tank, what type of surge can still occur and cause a roll over?
choice_a: Forward-and-backward surge
choice_b: Side-to-side surge
choice_c: Vertical surge
choice_d: No surge can occur in a baffled tank
explanation: The manual states side-to-side surge can still occur in baffled tanks, and this can cause a roll over.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.4 - Baffled Tanks

question: What are un-baffled liquid tankers sometimes called?
choice_a: "Smooth bore" tanks
choice_b: "Double-hulled" tanks
choice_c: "Vented" tanks
choice_d: "Pressurized" tanks
explanation: The manual states un-baffled liquid tankers are sometimes called "smooth bore" tanks.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 - Un-baffled Tanks

question: What do un-baffled tanks usually transport, according to the manual's example?
choice_a: Hazardous chemicals
choice_b: Dry bulk cement
choice_c: Food products, such as milk
choice_d: Compressed gases
explanation: The manual states un-baffled tanks are usually those that transport food products (milk, for example).
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 - Un-baffled Tanks

question: Why do sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles in tanks carrying food products?
choice_a: Because baffles reduce the tank's capacity too much
choice_b: Because baffles react chemically with food products
choice_c: Baffles are not actually forbidden in food-product tanks
choice_d: Because of the difficulty in cleaning the inside of the tank
explanation: The manual states sanitation regulations forbid the use of baffles because of the difficulty in cleaning the inside of the tank.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 - Un-baffled Tanks

question: When should you be extremely cautious (slow and careful) driving a smooth bore tank?
choice_a: Caution is not particularly needed with smooth bore tanks
choice_b: Only when the tank is completely full
choice_c: Especially when starting and stopping
choice_d: Only when driving uphill
explanation: The manual states to be extremely cautious (slow and careful) in driving smooth bore tanks, especially when starting and stopping.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.5 - Un-baffled Tanks

question: Why should you never load a cargo tank totally full?
choice_a: Liquids expand as they warm and you must leave room for the expanding liquid
choice_b: A totally full tank improves fuel economy
choice_c: It is only a concern when hauling hazardous materials
choice_d: Full tanks eliminate surge completely
explanation: The manual states: "Never load a cargo tank totally full. Liquids expand as they warm and you must leave room for the expanding liquid."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.6 - Outage

question: What is the term for the empty space left in a tank to allow for liquid expansion?
choice_a: Overfill margin
choice_b: Baffle gap
choice_c: Outage
choice_d: Bulkhead space
explanation: The manual states this is called "outage."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.6 - Outage

question: Do all liquids require the same amount of outage?
choice_a: Outage requirements are set entirely by the driver's discretion
choice_b: Yes, all liquids require exactly the same fixed percentage of outage
choice_c: No, since different liquids expand by different amounts, they require different amounts of outage
choice_d: Outage only applies to compressed gases, not liquids
explanation: The manual states since different liquids expand by different amounts, they require different amounts of outage, and you must know the outage requirement when hauling liquids in bulk.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.6 - Outage

question: Why might a full tank of a dense liquid, such as some acids, be a problem?
choice_a: It will not generate enough surge to be safe
choice_b: It will not fit through a standard manhole cover
choice_c: It may exceed legal weight limits
choice_d: It requires no outage at all
explanation: The manual states a full tank of dense liquid (such as some acids) may exceed legal weight limits, so you may often only partially fill tanks with heavy liquids.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.7 - How Much to Load?

question: According to the manual, what three things determine how much liquid you can load into a tank?
choice_a: The distance to be traveled, the driver's experience, and the road grade
choice_b: The amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits
choice_c: The color of the liquid, the tank material, and the weather
choice_d: The tank's age, its paint condition, and the manufacturer
explanation: The manual lists the amount to load as depending on: the amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.2.7 - How Much to Load?

question: Because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, how should you start, slow down, and stop a tank vehicle?
choice_a: In short, sharp bursts to keep the liquid settled
choice_b: It doesn't matter as long as you stay under the speed limit
choice_c: Very smoothly, with smooth turns and lane changes
choice_d: As quickly as possible to minimize time on the road
explanation: The manual states because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, you must start, slow down, and stop very smoothly, and also make smooth turns and lane changes.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.1 - Drive Smoothly

question: How should you use the brakes to help control surge when coming to a stop?
choice_a: Keep a steady pressure on the brakes and do not release too soon
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly
choice_c: Apply the parking brake while the vehicle is still moving
choice_d: Release the brakes immediately after applying them
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to keep a steady pressure on the brakes and not release too soon when coming to a stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 - Controlling Surge

question: What should you do regarding braking timing and following distance in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Brake as late as possible to save fuel
choice_b: Following distance is not affected by surge
choice_c: Brake far in advance of a stop and increase your following distance
choice_d: Decrease your following distance to compensate for surge
explanation: The manual states to brake far in advance of a stop and increase your following distance.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 - Controlling Surge

question: What braking methods should you use if you must make a quick stop to avoid a crash in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Controlled or stab braking
choice_b: Downshift only, without using the service brakes
choice_c: Pump the parking brake repeatedly
choice_d: Slam on the brakes as hard as possible
explanation: The manual states if you must make a quick stop to avoid a crash, use controlled or stab braking.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 - Controlling Surge

question: What does the manual warn can happen if you steer quickly while braking a tank vehicle?
choice_a: The surge will be eliminated instantly
choice_b: Your vehicle may roll over
choice_c: The vehicle will automatically stabilize itself
choice_d: Nothing, tank vehicles are roll-resistant when braking
explanation: The manual states to remember that if you steer quickly while braking, your vehicle may roll over.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.2 - Controlling Surge

question: How should you approach curves while driving a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Slow down before the curve, then accelerate slightly through the curve
choice_b: Maintain a constant speed throughout the curve
choice_c: Accelerate before the curve and brake through it
choice_d: Brake heavily throughout the entire curve
explanation: The manual states to slow down before curves, then accelerate slightly through the curve.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.3 - Curves

question: What does the manual say about the posted speed for a curve when driving a tank vehicle?
choice_a: It is always too slow for a tank vehicle
choice_b: It may be too fast for a tank vehicle
choice_c: It is irrelevant since tank vehicles ignore posted speeds
choice_d: It is always exactly right for tank vehicles
explanation: The manual states the posted speed for a curve may be too fast for a tank vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.3 - Curves

question: How do wet roads affect the stopping distance of a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Wet roads cut the normal stopping distance in half
choice_b: Wet roads double the normal stopping distance
choice_c: Wet roads have no effect on stopping distance
choice_d: Wet roads only affect stopping distance on curves
explanation: The manual states to remember that wet roads double the normal stopping distance.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.4 - Stopping Distance

question: According to the manual, which tank vehicles may take longer to stop?
choice_a: Full tank vehicles always stop faster regardless of load
choice_b: Empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones
choice_c: Tank vehicles stop the same as any other vehicle regardless of load
choice_d: Load status has no effect on stopping distance
explanation: The manual states empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.4 - Stopping Distance

question: What driving behaviors does the manual warn can cause a tank vehicle to skid?
choice_a: Using controlled or stab braking correctly
choice_b: Keeping a steady pressure on the brakes
choice_c: Over steering, over accelerating, or over braking
choice_d: Driving too slowly for conditions
explanation: The manual states: "Don't over steer, over accelerate, or over brake. If you do, your vehicle may skid."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.5 - Skids

question: On tank trailers, what may happen if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid?
choice_a: The vehicle may jackknife
choice_b: The vehicle will automatically correct itself
choice_c: The baffles will engage automatically to stop the skid
choice_d: The tank will vent excess pressure safely
explanation: The manual states on tank trailers, if your drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, your vehicle may jackknife, and when any vehicle starts to skid you must take action to restore traction to the wheels.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, 8.3.5 - Skids
